goals: State the Kossel–Lewis approach and the octet rule, and write Lewis symbols using valence electrons
Draw electron-dot structures of NaCl, Li₂O, MgO, CaO, MgF₂ and Na₂S and predict the formula of an ionic compound
Explain the conditions that favour an ionic bond: ionisation enthalpy, electron gain enthalpy, lattice enthalpy and electronegativity difference

slides.narration: Welcome. In this part we ask why atoms form bonds at all, and we meet the simplest answer, given by Kossel and Lewis. Then we follow a sodium atom giving one electron to a chlorine atom, and see how that single transfer creates two ions which attract each other strongly.

slides.heading: Valence electrons and the Kossel–Lewis approach
slides.body_md: **Valence electrons** are the electrons of the outermost shell; they alone take part in bonding. Kossel and Lewis explained bonding by the **stability of the noble gases**: their outer shells are full, and other atoms reach the same arrangement by **gaining, losing or sharing** electrons.

visual.alt: Table of the number of valence electrons for the main groups

slides.narration: Valence electrons are the electrons of the outermost shell, and only these take part in bonding. The number equals the group number for the first two groups, and the group number minus ten for the groups thirteen to eighteen. Kossel and Lewis said that atoms combine so as to reach the full outer shell of a noble gas.

slides.heading: The octet rule
slides.body_md: Atoms tend to combine until each has **eight electrons** in its outermost shell (the **octet rule**); hydrogen, lithium and beryllium aim for **two**, like helium. An atom can reach an octet by **transfer** (electrovalent or ionic bond) or by **sharing** (covalent bond).

nodes.label: Atom has an incomplete outer shell
Metal loses electrons to a non-metal: ionic bond
Two non-metals share electron pairs: covalent bond
Each atom reaches 8 outer electrons (2 for H)

visual.alt: Flow chart showing that an atom reaches an octet either by electron transfer to give an ionic bond or by sharing to give a covalent bond

slides.narration: The octet rule says that atoms combine until each has eight electrons in the outer shell. Hydrogen, lithium and beryllium instead aim for two, like helium. There are two ways to get there. A metal can hand electrons over to a non-metal, giving an ionic bond, or two non-metals can share electrons, giving a covalent bond.

slides.heading: Sodium chloride by electron transfer
slides.body_md: Sodium (2, 8, 1) gives its **one valence electron** to chlorine (2, 8, 7). Na⁺ has the neon arrangement (2, 8) and Cl⁻ has the argon arrangement (2, 8, 8). The **electrostatic attraction** between these opposite charges is the **ionic bond**.

slides.narration: Look at the dots. Sodium has one valence electron and chlorine has seven. Sodium gives its electron to chlorine, shown by the green arrow. Both atoms now have a full outer shell of eight electrons. The sodium ion is positive, the chloride ion is negative, and the attraction between them is the ionic bond.

slides.heading: Quick check: octet or duplet?
slides.body_md: Count the electrons in the outermost occupied shell of each ion.
slides.narration: Quick check. For each ion, work out how many electrons it has left by taking the charge away from the atomic number, then write the arrangement in shells. Decide which ion ends with a duplet like helium rather than an octet like neon or argon.

slides.heading: Writing the electron-dot structure of an ionic compound
slides.body_md: **1.** Draw the Lewis symbol of each atom. **2.** Move electrons from the metal to the non-metal until the non-metal has eight. **3.** Show each ion in **brackets with its charge**; the cation shows no outer electrons, the anion shows eight dots. **4.** Check that the **total charge is zero**.

nodes.label: Count valence electrons of each atom
Metal gives up all its valence electrons
Non-metal takes 8 minus its valence electrons
Balance the numbers of ions so that charges cancel
Write brackets, charges and eight dots on the anion

visual.alt: Flow chart of the steps for writing an electron-dot structure of an ionic compound

slides.narration: Here are the steps. Count the valence electrons of each atom. The metal gives up all of its valence electrons. The non-metal takes as many as it needs to reach eight. Adjust the numbers of ions until the total charge is zero. Finally draw each ion in square brackets with its charge, and show eight dots on the anion.

slides.heading: Electron-dot structures of five ionic compounds
slides.body_md: In **Li₂O** two Li atoms give one electron each to O. In **MgO** and **CaO** two electrons pass to O. In **MgF₂** the Mg atom gives one electron to each of two F atoms. In **Na₂S** each of two Na atoms gives one electron to S.

slides.heading: Worked example: formula of magnesium nitride
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Magnesium (2 valence electrons) burns in nitrogen (5 valence electrons). Predict the formula and the number of electrons transferred.

Mg loses 2 electrons: $\ce{Mg -> Mg^2+ + 2e-}$. N needs $8 - 5 = 3$: $\ce{N + 3e- -> N^3-}$. The least common multiple of 2 and 3 is 6, so **3 Mg** lose 3 × 2 = 6 electrons and **2 N** gain 2 × 3 = 6. Charge: $3(+2) + 2(-3) = 0$. Formula: $\ce{Mg3N2}$, with **6** electrons transferred.

rows: Electrons lost or gained per atom

visual.alt: Table of the electron balance for magnesium nitride

slides.narration: Magnesium has two valence electrons, so it loses two. Nitrogen has five, so it needs three. The lowest common multiple of two and three is six. So three magnesium atoms give away six electrons, and two nitrogen atoms take six. The charges cancel, and the formula is magnesium nitride with three magnesium and two nitrogen.

slides.heading: Conditions for forming an ionic bond
slides.body_md: An ionic bond forms easily when **(1)** the metal has a **low ionisation enthalpy**, **(2)** the non-metal has a **large negative electron gain enthalpy**, **(3)** the **lattice enthalpy** released on packing the ions is high (high charges, small ions), and **(4)** the **electronegativity difference** is large (above about 1.7).

rows: Electron gain enthalpy of the non-metal

visual.alt: Table of the four conditions that favour an ionic bond

slides.narration: Four things favour an ionic bond. The metal should lose electrons easily, so its ionisation enthalpy is low. The non-metal should gain electrons readily, so its electron gain enthalpy is large and negative. The lattice enthalpy should be high, and the difference in electronegativity should be large, above about one point seven.

slides.heading: Electronegativity difference
slides.body_md: A bond between atoms with a **large difference in electronegativity** (Na–Cl 2.1, Mg–O 2.3, Ca–F 3.0) is ionic, since the more electronegative atom pulls the electron away completely. C–H (0.4) is covalent.

slides.heading: Worked example: energy to make an ion pair
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Compare the energy needed to form gaseous ion pairs from atoms: $\ce{Na(g) + Cl(g) -> Na+(g) + Cl-(g)}$ and $\ce{K(g) + Cl(g) -> K+(g) + Cl-(g)}$. Ionisation enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹): Na 496, K 419; electron gain enthalpy of Cl −349.

**Na–Cl:** 496 + (−349) = **+147** kJ mol⁻¹. **K–Cl:** 419 + (−349) = **+70** kJ mol⁻¹. Both are positive, but the lattice enthalpy pays for them: 147 + (-788) = -641 and 70 + (-717) = -647 kJ mol⁻¹.

visual.alt: Table of the energy of ion-pair formation, lattice enthalpy and the sum for NaCl and KCl

slides.narration: Add the ionisation enthalpy of the metal to the electron gain enthalpy of chlorine. The result is positive in both cases, so forming gaseous ions from atoms costs energy. The compound still forms because the lattice enthalpy is a large negative number. The sum of the two is negative, so each solid is more stable than its separate atoms.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Valence electrons = outer-shell electrons; Kossel–Lewis: atoms reach a noble gas arrangement by transfer or sharing.
Octet rule: 8 outer electrons (2 for H, Li, Be).
Ionic bond = electrostatic attraction between ions formed by electron transfer; metal gives, non-metal takes.
Dot structures: cation in brackets with no dots, anion with 8 dots, total charge zero.
Favoured by low IE, large negative EGE, high lattice enthalpy and a large electronegativity difference (about 1.7 or more).

visual.alt: Summary table of the ions and electrons moved for the compounds of Part 1

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. Valence electrons are those of the outer shell. Atoms combine to reach eight electrons, or two for the smallest atoms. In an ionic bond a metal gives electrons to a non-metal, and the oppositely charged ions attract. Low ionisation enthalpy, large negative electron gain enthalpy, high lattice enthalpy and a large electronegativity difference all favour it.

slides.narration: Welcome to Part 2. Some metals form a single ion, but iron, tin and lead can form two. We shall find the reasons in their electron configurations. Then we meet lattice enthalpy, the energy that holds an ionic crystal together, and learn to calculate it from a Born-Haber cycle.

slides.heading: Formation of cations and anions
slides.body_md: A **cation** forms when an atom loses electrons; it is **smaller** than the atom, because the outer shell goes and the same nuclear charge holds fewer electrons. An **anion** forms when an atom gains electrons; it is **larger**, because repulsion rises while the nuclear charge is unchanged.

visual.alt: Table of ion formation with the change in radius

slides.narration: A cation forms when an atom loses electrons. It is smaller than the atom, because the outer shell has gone and the same nuclear charge holds fewer electrons. An anion forms when an atom gains electrons. It is larger than the atom, because the extra electron repels the others while the nuclear charge stays the same.

slides.heading: Variable electrovalency: two causes
slides.body_md: Some elements form **more than one cation**. In the **d-block** (Fe²⁺, Fe³⁺) the core left after the s electrons go is **not a stable noble gas core**, so d electrons can be lost too (**unstable core**). In heavy **p-block** elements (Tl⁺, Sn²⁺, Pb²⁺) the **ns² pair resists loss** (**inert pair effect**).

visual.alt: Table of the two causes of variable electrovalency

slides.narration: Variable electrovalency has two common causes. In the d block, the core that remains after the s electrons are lost is not a stable noble gas core, so d electrons may be lost as well. In heavy p block elements, the pair of s electrons is held so tightly that it often stays, which makes the lower oxidation state more stable.

slides.heading: Iron and lead in orbital boxes
slides.body_md: **Iron:** [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². Loss of 4s² gives **Fe²⁺** (3d⁶); loss of one 3d electron gives **Fe³⁺** (3d⁵, half-filled). **Lead:** 6s² 6p². Loss of 6p² gives **Pb²⁺**; if the **6s² pair** is lost too, **Pb⁴⁺** results.

slides.heading: Quick check: electrons in tin ions
slides.body_md: Take the charge away from the atomic number.
slides.narration: Quick check. An ion has the atomic number minus its charge in electrons. Work this out for tin with a two plus charge and with a four plus charge, and decide which electrons have been lost in each case, the p electrons or also the s pair.

slides.heading: The inert pair effect down a group
slides.body_md: Going down Groups 13, 14 and 15, the two ns electrons are **less and less involved in bonding** because they are poorly shielded and held close to the nucleus. The state **two less than the group valence** becomes **more stable**: +1 for Tl, +2 for Pb, +3 for Bi. Pb(IV) compounds are **oxidising**; Pb(II) compounds are stable.

visual.alt: Table of the inert pair effect for Tl, Sn, Pb and Bi

slides.narration: Down the p block the pair of s electrons becomes more and more reluctant to take part in bonding. So thallium prefers plus one, lead prefers plus two, and bismuth prefers plus three. Lead four compounds are oxidising agents, because lead would rather go back to the plus two state.

slides.heading: Lattice enthalpy
slides.body_md: The **lattice enthalpy** is the enthalpy change when **one mole of an ionic solid is formed from its gaseous ions**, e.g. $\ce{Na+(g) + Cl-(g) -> NaCl(s)}$, $-788$ kJ mol⁻¹. It is larger for ions of **higher charge** and **smaller radius**.

visual.alt: Table of lattice enthalpies with the ions concerned

slides.narration: Lattice enthalpy is the energy change when one mole of an ionic solid forms from its gaseous ions. It is a large negative number. It is greater for ions with higher charges and smaller radii. Compare sodium fluoride with sodium iodide: the smaller fluoride ion gives the larger lattice enthalpy.

slides.heading: The Born–Haber cycle for sodium chloride

slides.heading: Worked example: lattice enthalpy of NaCl
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Find the lattice enthalpy of NaCl from: $\Delta H_\text{f} = -412$; sublimation of Na 108; Cl–Cl dissociation 242 (per mole of Cl₂); ionisation of Na 496; electron gain of Cl -349 (all kJ mol⁻¹).

$\Delta H_\text{f} = \Delta H_\text{sub} + \tfrac12 D + \text{IE} + \text{EGE} + U$

$-412 = 108 + 121 + 496 + (-349) + U$, so $U = -412 - 376 = -788$ kJ mol⁻¹.

visual.alt: Table of the Born-Haber steps for NaCl with running totals

slides.narration: Write the enthalpy of formation as the sum of all the steps. The first four steps add up to plus three hundred seventy six kilojoules. The enthalpy of formation is minus four hundred twelve, so the lattice enthalpy must be the difference, minus seven hundred eighty eight kilojoules per mole. slides.heading: Worked example: lattice enthalpy of MgCl₂
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** For $\ce{MgCl2}$: $\Delta H_\text{f} = -641$; sublimation of Mg 148; Cl₂ dissociation 242; IE₁ 738; IE₂ 1451; electron gain of Cl -349 (kJ mol⁻¹). Find $U$.

Steps: $148 + 242 + 738 + 1451 + 2(-349) = 1881$ kJ mol⁻¹. $U = -641 - 1881 = -2522$ kJ mol⁻¹ (tabulated Born–Haber values lie near −2526 because of the rounding of the data).

The total is plus one thousand eight hundred eighty one kilojoules. Subtract it from the enthalpy of formation, minus six hundred forty one, to get a lattice enthalpy of about minus two thousand five hundred twenty two kilojoules per mole.

slides.heading: Characteristics of ionic compounds
slides.body_md: Ionic solids are **hard, brittle crystals with high melting and boiling points**. They are **soluble in polar solvents** such as water, **insoluble in non-polar** solvents, and **conduct only when molten or dissolved**. All follow from a lattice of ions held by strong electrostatic forces.

slides.narration: Ionic compounds are hard, brittle crystals with high melting points. They dissolve in water, because water molecules surround the ions, but not in non-polar solvents. They conduct electricity when melted or dissolved, but not as solids. All of this follows from a rigid lattice of ions held by strong electrostatic attraction.

slides.heading: Why the melt conducts but the solid does not
slides.body_md: In the **solid** the ions sit in fixed positions, so no charge can flow. In the **melt** (and in solution) the ions are **free**: cations move to the negative electrode and anions to the positive electrode, carrying the current.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Cation: smaller than its atom; anion: larger than its atom.
Variable electrovalency: unstable core (Fe²⁺, Fe³⁺ with half-filled 3d⁵) and inert pair effect (Tl⁺, Sn²⁺, Pb²⁺, Bi³⁺).

notes.title: Ionic Bonding — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Valence electrons, the Kossel–Lewis approach and the octet rule
sections.body_md:
**Valence electrons** are the electrons in the outermost shell of an atom; they are the ones that take part in bonding. A **Lewis symbol** shows them as dots round the symbol of the element (singly on four sides first, then paired).

**Kossel and Lewis (1916)** explained bonding by the stability of the noble gases, whose outer shells are complete (8 electrons; 2 for helium). Other atoms reach such an arrangement by **transfer** of electrons (**electrovalent** or ionic bond, between a metal and a non-metal) or by **sharing** of electrons (**covalent** bond, between non-metals). The tendency to have eight electrons in the outermost shell is the **octet rule**; hydrogen, lithium and beryllium reach a **duplet** (two electrons), like helium.

key_terms.definition_md: The electrons of the outermost shell, which take part in bonding.
Atoms combine so that each has eight electrons in its outermost shell (two for H, Li, Be).
The symbol of an element with dots for its valence electrons.

visual.alt: Table of valence electrons and the usual route to an octet for the main groups

sections.heading: 2. The ionic bond and electron-dot structures
sections.body_md:
An **ionic (electrovalent) bond** is the electrostatic attraction between the positive and negative ions formed when a metal transfers electrons to a non-metal. In an electron-dot structure the cation is shown in brackets with its charge and **no dots** (its outer shell has been lost), and the anion in brackets with **eight dots** and its charge. The number of ions is chosen so that the **total charge is zero**: electrons lost = electrons gained.

NaCl: Na gives 1 e⁻ to Cl. $\ce{Li2O}$, $\ce{Na2S}$: two metal atoms give 1 e⁻ each. MgO, CaO: 2 e⁻. $\ce{MgF2}$: Mg gives 1 e⁻ to each of two F. Formula rule: with metal charge $q_c$ and non-metal charge $q_a$, the ratio of cations to anions is $q_a : q_c$ (in lowest terms).

key_terms.definition_md: The bond formed by the electrostatic attraction between ions produced by electron transfer.
Having the same number of electrons, e.g. Na⁺, Mg²⁺, F⁻ and O²⁻ (10 electrons).

sections.heading: 3. Conditions for the formation of an ionic bond
sections.body_md: Ionic bonds form readily when: **(1)** the metal has a **low ionisation enthalpy**; **(2)** the non-metal has a **large negative electron gain enthalpy**; **(3)** the **lattice enthalpy** is high (ions of high charge and small size); **(4)** the **electronegativity difference** is large, about **1.7 or more**. Making the gaseous ions from atoms usually absorbs energy (Na–Cl: 496 + (-349) = +147 kJ mol⁻¹); it is the **lattice enthalpy** that makes the compound stable.

key_terms.definition_md: The enthalpy change to remove an electron from a gaseous atom or ion.
The enthalpy change when a gaseous atom gains an electron (negative for most non-metals).

sections.heading: 4. Cations, anions and variable electrovalency
sections.body_md:
A **cation is smaller** than its parent atom (the outer shell is lost and the same nuclear charge holds fewer electrons); an **anion is larger** (more electron repulsion, same nuclear charge).

Some elements form more than one cation (**variable electrovalency**). **Unstable core:** after loss of the ns electrons, the d-block atom is left with an incomplete d core that is not a noble gas core, so d electrons may go too: Fe ([Ar] 3d⁶ 4s²) gives Fe²⁺ (3d⁶) and Fe³⁺ (3d⁵, half-filled). **Inert pair effect:** in heavy p-block elements the ns² pair (poorly shielded, close to the nucleus) is slow to take part in bonding, so the state two below the group valence is more stable: Tl⁺, Sn²⁺ and Pb²⁺, Bi³⁺. Pb(IV) is oxidising; Pb(II) is stable.

key_terms.definition_md: The ability of an element to form more than one stable cation.
An inner core of electrons (incomplete d subshell) that is not a stable noble gas arrangement, so more electrons can be lost.
The reluctance of the ns² electrons of heavy p-block elements to take part in bonding.

sections.heading: 5. Lattice enthalpy and the Born–Haber cycle
sections.body_md:
The **lattice enthalpy** $U$ is the enthalpy change when **one mole of a solid is formed from its gaseous ions**; it is negative and larger for ions with **higher charge** and **smaller radius** (NaF −923 > NaCl −788 > NaI −700 kJ mol⁻¹; MgO −3791).

The **Born–Haber cycle** applies **Hess's law**: $\Delta H_\text{f} = \Delta H_\text{sub} + \tfrac12 D + \text{IE} + \text{EGE} + U$ (use $\tfrac12 D$ for one mole of X atoms from X₂, and multiply IE and EGE steps for 2+ ions or 2 X atoms). For NaCl: $108 + 121 + 496 + (-349) + U = -412$ gives $U = -788$ kJ mol⁻¹. For $\ce{MgCl2}$ with ΔHf = −641 kJ mol⁻¹ the steps total +1881 and $U = -2522$ kJ mol⁻¹.

key_terms.definition_md: The enthalpy change when one mole of an ionic solid is formed from its gaseous ions.
The enthalpy change of a reaction is the same whether it takes place in one step or in several.
A Hess’s-law cycle linking the enthalpy of formation of an ionic solid to atomisation, ionisation, electron gain and lattice enthalpies.

sections.heading: 6. Characteristics of electrovalent compounds
sections.body_md: **Physical state:** hard crystalline solids. **Melting and boiling points:** high, since strong electrostatic forces act in all directions. **Brittle:** a blow shifts a layer so like ions face each other and repel. **Solubility:** dissolve in polar solvents such as water (hydration of ions releases energy) and not in non-polar solvents. **Conductivity:** solid does not conduct (ions fixed); molten and aqueous conduct (ions free). **Reactions:** ionic reactions in solution are fast, because the ions are already present.

key_terms.definition_md: The tendency of a crystal to split under a blow; in ionic solids it comes from repulsion between like ions after a layer slips.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Showing dots inside the bracket of a cation, or fewer than eight dots on an anion.
- Writing charges that do not cancel, or the wrong ratio of ions (Mg₃N₂, Al₂O₃, MgF₂).
- Using the full Cl–Cl dissociation enthalpy in the NaCl cycle instead of half.
- Forgetting the second ionisation enthalpy of magnesium or doubling the electron gain enthalpy for two Cl.
- Explaining conduction by electrons instead of ions, or saying ionic solids are brittle because the bonds are weak.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Electron-dot structure: transfer shown (1), ions in brackets with charges and eight dots (1), formula or configuration (1).
- Born–Haber numericals: each step with its sign and the half-dissociation enthalpy (1), the sum (1), the lattice enthalpy with units (1).
- Variable electrovalency: configurations of both ions (1) and the named reason, unstable core or inert pair (1).

cards.front_md: What are valence electrons?
cards.back_md: The electrons in the outermost shell; they take part in bonding.

cards.front_md: State the octet rule.
cards.back_md: Atoms combine so that each has eight electrons in its outermost shell.

cards.front_md: Which atoms aim for a duplet?
cards.back_md: H, Li and Be: two electrons, like helium.

cards.front_md: Why are noble gases unreactive (Kossel–Lewis)?
cards.back_md: Their outer shells are complete (8 electrons; 2 for He).

cards.front_md: Two ways an atom can reach an octet?
cards.back_md: Transfer of electrons (ionic bond) or sharing (covalent bond).

cards.front_md: How many dots in the Lewis symbol of a Group 16 atom?
cards.back_md: Six: two pairs and two single dots.

cards.front_md: What is an ionic (electrovalent) bond?
cards.back_md: The electrostatic attraction between ions formed by electron transfer.

cards.front_md: How is a cation shown in an electron-dot structure?
cards.back_md: In brackets with its charge and no outer dots.

cards.front_md: How is an anion shown?
cards.back_md: In brackets with eight dots and its charge.

cards.front_md: What happens in the formation of Na₂S?
cards.back_md: Each of two Na atoms gives 1 electron to S, giving 2 Na⁺ and S²⁻.

cards.front_md: What happens in the formation of MgF₂?
cards.back_md: Mg gives 1 electron to each of two F atoms: Mg²⁺ and 2 F⁻.

cards.front_md: Formula of the compound of Al and O?
cards.back_md: $\ce{Al2O3}$: 6 electrons move (2 Al lose 6, 3 O gain 6).

cards.front_md: Four conditions favouring an ionic bond?
cards.back_md: Low IE of the metal, large negative EGE of the non-metal, high lattice enthalpy, large electronegativity difference.

cards.front_md: Electronegativity difference above which a bond is mainly ionic?
cards.back_md: About 1.7.

cards.front_md: Why does NaCl form although IE + EGE is positive (+147 kJ mol⁻¹)?
cards.back_md: The lattice enthalpy, −788 kJ mol⁻¹, releases far more energy.

cards.front_md: Is a cation larger or smaller than its atom? Why?
cards.back_md: Smaller: the outer shell is lost and the same nuclear charge holds fewer electrons.

cards.front_md: Is an anion larger or smaller than its atom? Why?
cards.back_md: Larger: more electron repulsion, same nuclear charge.

cards.front_md: What is variable electrovalency?
cards.back_md: The ability of an element to form more than one stable cation.

cards.front_md: What is an unstable core?
cards.back_md: An incomplete d core that is not a noble gas arrangement, so more electrons can be lost (Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺).

cards.front_md: Why is Fe³⁺ stable?
cards.back_md: Its 3d⁵ arrangement is half-filled.

cards.front_md: What is the inert pair effect?
cards.back_md: The ns² electrons of heavy p-block elements resist taking part in bonding.

cards.front_md: Which oxidation state is more stable for Pb, Tl?
Electrons in Pb⁴⁺ (Z = 82)?
Define lattice enthalpy.
cards.back_md: The enthalpy change when one mole of a solid is formed from its gaseous ions.

cards.front_md: What makes the lattice enthalpy larger?
cards.back_md: Higher ionic charges and smaller ionic radii.

cards.front_md: On which law is the Born–Haber cycle based?
cards.back_md: Hess’s law.

cards.front_md: Write the Born–Haber sum for a 1 : 1 halide MX.
cards.back_md: $\Delta H_\text{f} = \Delta H_\text{sub} + \tfrac12 D + \text{IE} + \text{EGE} + U$.

cards.front_md: Lattice enthalpy of NaCl from the cycle?
What changes for MgCl₂ in the cycle?
cards.back_md: Two ionisation steps, 2 × EGE, and a whole Cl–Cl dissociation enthalpy for two Cl atoms.

cards.front_md: Why is an ionic crystal brittle?
cards.back_md: A shifted layer brings like ions face to face, and they repel.

cards.front_md: Why does a molten ionic compound conduct but not the solid?
cards.back_md: Ions are free to move in the melt but fixed in the solid lattice.

cards.front_md: Why do ionic compounds dissolve in water?
cards.back_md: Hydration of the ions by polar water molecules releases enough energy to overcome the lattice enthalpy.

questions.stem_md: A water-treatment chemist is told that the sample contains the non-metal of atomic number 16. How many valence electrons does an atom of this element have?
questions.solution_md: Z = 16 gives the configuration 2, 8, 6, so the outermost (valence) shell holds 6 electrons — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which statement agrees with the Kossel–Lewis explanation of why atoms of most elements join to form compounds?

options.text_md: Atoms transfer or share electrons so that each acquires the outer-shell arrangement of the nearest noble gas
Atoms join so that each nucleus gains extra protons from its neighbour
Atoms join so that the number of neutrons in each nucleus becomes equal
Atoms join to lose their valence electrons completely and become neutral again

questions.solution_md: Kossel and Lewis proposed that the stability of the noble gases comes from their full outer shells, and that other atoms reach such an arrangement by gaining, losing or sharing electrons — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A student studying battery and fertiliser materials works out the electron arrangements of four ions found in them. Which of these ions does NOT have eight electrons in its outermost occupied shell?

options.text_md: Li⁺
Mg²⁺
Cl⁻
O²⁻

questions.solution_md: Li⁺ has 3 − 1 = 2 electrons, arranged (2), a duplet like helium, not an octet. Mg²⁺ (2, 8), Cl⁻ (2, 8, 8) and O²⁻ (2, 8) each have 8 electrons in the outer shell — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The Lewis (electron-dot) symbol of the element in Group 15 of the periodic table, drawn for a fertiliser-chemistry class, shows:

options.text_md: three dots round the symbol, all single
five dots round the symbol, all single
five dots round the symbol, one pair and three single dots
eight dots round the symbol, four pairs

questions.solution_md: A Group 15 atom has 5 valence electrons. Dots are placed singly on the four sides first and then paired, giving one pair and three single dots — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A helium atom is stable because its outermost shell holds an octet of eight electrons.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Helium has only the first shell, which is complete with 2 electrons (a duplet); its stability does not come from an octet.

questions.stem_md: The Lewis symbol of any alkaline earth metal shows ___ dots.
questions.solution_md: Alkaline earth metals (Group 2) have two valence electrons, so their Lewis symbols show two dots.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Neon and argon take part in very few chemical reactions.

**Reason (R):** The outermost shell of each of these atoms already holds eight electrons.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true, and the full outer shell is the reason for the low reactivity, so R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: State the octet rule. Why do hydrogen and lithium form stable ions or molecules with only two electrons in the outer shell?

answer.model_answer_md: Atoms tend to enter into chemical combination, by losing, gaining or sharing electrons, so that each acquires eight electrons in its outermost shell, the arrangement of a noble gas. Hydrogen and lithium have only the first shell as the nearest filled shell (helium), which is complete with two electrons, so they attain a duplet instead of an octet.

questions.solution_md: Octet statement; duplet like helium.

marking_scheme.step: Duplet: first shell complete with two electrons, like helium

questions.stem_md: Give three ideas of the Kossel–Lewis approach to chemical bonding.

answer.model_answer_md: First, in every atom the valence electrons, those of the outermost shell, take part in bonding. Second, the noble gases are stable (inert) because their outer shells are complete, 8 electrons (2 for helium). Third, other atoms form bonds, by transfer of electrons (electrovalent bond) or by sharing electrons (covalent bond), so as to reach this noble gas arrangement of eight electrons, the octet rule.

questions.solution_md: Valence electrons; noble gas stability; transfer or sharing to an octet.

marking_scheme.step: Valence electrons take part in bonding
Transfer or sharing to complete the octet

questions.stem_md: During the formation of sodium chloride from its atoms, the electron arrangements of sodium and chlorine change from (2, 8, 1) and (2, 8, 7) to:

options.text_md: (2, 8, 2) for the sodium ion and (2, 8, 6) for the chloride ion
(2, 8) for the sodium ion and (2, 8, 8) for the chloride ion
(2, 8) for the sodium ion and (2, 8, 6) for the chloride ion
(2, 8, 8) for the sodium ion and (2, 8) for the chloride ion

questions.solution_md: Na gives its single outer electron to Cl: Na⁺ is (2, 8) and Cl⁻ is (2, 8, 8) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In the electron-dot structure of lithium oxide used in a ceramics lab, which description is correct?

options.text_md: One Li⁺ ion and one O⁻ ion, each with eight dots
Two Li⁺ ions with no outer electrons and one O²⁻ ion with eight dots in brackets
Two Li⁺ ions each with eight dots and one O²⁻ ion with six dots
Two Li atoms each sharing one pair of dots with an oxygen atom

questions.solution_md: Each of two Li atoms transfers one electron to O, which then has 6 + 2 = 8 outer electrons. Li⁺ has no outer electrons (it is a helium duplet) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A refractory brick is made from the compound of aluminium (three valence electrons) and oxygen (six valence electrons). Predicting the formula by electron transfer, the compound is:

options.text_md: $\ce{Al2O3}$, with 6 electrons transferred in all
$\ce{AlO}$, with 3 electrons transferred in all
$\ce{Al3O2}$, with 9 electrons transferred in all
$\ce{Al2O}$, with 6 electrons transferred in all

questions.solution_md: Al gives 3 electrons, O takes 2, so the least common multiple is 6: 2 Al and 3 O, $\ce{Al2O3}$, with 6 electrons transferred in all — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Calcium metal burns in nitrogen to form a nitride. In forming one formula unit of the product, the total number of electrons transferred from calcium atoms to nitrogen atoms is:
questions.solution_md: Ca gives 2 electrons and N takes 3, so the formula is $\ce{Ca3N2}$: 3 Ca lose $3 \times 2 = 6$ and 2 N gain $2 \times 3 = 6$ — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which set of properties of the two reacting elements most favours the formation of a stable ionic compound?

options.text_md: A low ionisation enthalpy for the metal, a large negative electron gain enthalpy for the non-metal and a high lattice enthalpy of the product
A high ionisation enthalpy for the metal, a small electron gain enthalpy for the non-metal and a low lattice enthalpy
A low ionisation enthalpy for the metal, a positive electron gain enthalpy for the non-metal and a low lattice enthalpy
A high ionisation enthalpy for the metal, a large negative electron gain enthalpy for the non-metal and a high lattice enthalpy

questions.solution_md: The metal must lose electrons easily (low IE), the non-metal must gain them easily (large negative EGE) and the energy released when the ions pack into a lattice must be high — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Pauling electronegativities (given) are K 0.8, Cl 3, C 2.5, O 3.5, H 2.1, Br 2.8 and N 3. Which pair of atoms is most likely to form an ionic bond in the solid state?

options.text_md: C and O (difference 1.0)
H and Br (difference 0.7)
N and Cl (difference 0.0)
K and Cl (difference 2.2)

questions.solution_md: The differences are 2.2, 1.0, 0.7, 0.0. Only K–Cl, between a very electropositive metal and a very electronegative non-metal, has a large enough difference (well above 1.7) for electron transfer — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A dentist’s fluoride varnish contains magnesium fluoride. In its electron-dot structure the charges and the numbers of the ions are:

options.text_md: two Mg²⁺ ions and one F²⁻ ion
one Mg⁺ ion and one F⁻ ion
one Mg²⁺ ion and two F⁻ ions, each F⁻ with eight dots
one Mg²⁺ ion and two F⁻ ions, each F⁻ with seven dots

questions.solution_md: Mg gives 2 electrons; each F takes 1 and then has 7 + 1 = 8 outer electrons, so one Mg²⁺ pairs with two F⁻ — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? In the formation of sodium sulfide, the sulfur atom gains two electrons, one from each of two sodium atoms.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. Sulfur has 6 valence electrons and needs 2 more for an octet; each sodium atom gives one, so the formula is Na₂S.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Two electrons are transferred from a magnesium atom to an oxygen atom when magnesium oxide forms.

**Reason (R):** Magnesium oxide is a white solid with a very high melting point.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Mg has two valence electrons and O needs two, so A is true; R is also a true property of MgO, but it says nothing about the number of electrons transferred, so it is not the explanation — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Chlorine releases energy when a gaseous atom gains one electron.

**Reason (R):** The electron gain enthalpy of chlorine is large and positive.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true: the first electron gain enthalpy of Cl is about −349 kJ mol⁻¹ (energy is released). R is false because the value is negative — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** An ionic compound can be formed only between a Group 1 metal and a halogen.

**Reason (R):** Every metal-to-non-metal combination involves the transfer of exactly one electron.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is false: MgO, CaO and Na₂S, for example, are ionic. R is false: electrons transferred range from one to three or more — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Match each ionic compound with the ions that appear in its electron-dot structure.

options.text_md: Li₂O
MgO
MgF₂
Na₂S

questions.solution_md: Li₂O → r (two Li⁺ and one O²⁻); MgO → p (one Mg²⁺ and one O²⁻); MgF₂ → s (one Mg²⁺ and two F⁻); Na₂S → q (two Na⁺ and one S²⁻).

questions.stem_md: Show by electron-dot structures how calcium oxide is formed from a calcium atom and an oxygen atom. Give the number of electrons in the outer shell of each ion formed.

answer.model_answer_md: A calcium atom (2, 8, 8, 2) has two valence electrons, drawn as two dots; an oxygen atom (2, 6) has six. Calcium transfers both electrons to oxygen: Ca• • + O (six dots) → [Ca]²⁺ [O with eight dots]²⁻. The Ca²⁺ ion has the argon arrangement, 8 electrons in the outer shell, and the O²⁻ ion has the neon arrangement, also 8.

questions.solution_md: Two electrons from Ca to O; Ca²⁺ (2, 8, 8) and O²⁻ (2, 8).

marking_scheme.step: Transfer of two electrons from Ca to O shown
Ions in brackets with charges and eight outer electrons each

questions.stem_md: Name two factors that favour the formation of an ionic bond between a metal and a non-metal, and say how each acts.

answer.model_answer_md: A low ionisation enthalpy of the metal favours the loss of electrons to give the cation, so less energy has to be supplied. A large negative electron gain enthalpy of the non-metal favours formation of the anion. (A high lattice enthalpy, and a large difference in electronegativity, also favour it: the energy released when the ions pack into a crystal pays for the energy needed to form them.)

questions.solution_md: Low ionisation enthalpy; large negative electron gain enthalpy (or high lattice enthalpy).

questions.stem_md: Sodium and magnesium each burn in chlorine. Write the formula of each product, show the electrons transferred, and explain why one magnesium atom needs two chlorine atoms.

answer.model_answer_md: Sodium gives one electron to one Cl atom: $\ce{Na -> Na+ + e-}$, $\ce{Cl + e- -> Cl-}$, giving $\ce{NaCl}$. Magnesium has two valence electrons and gives both: $\ce{Mg -> Mg^2+ + 2e-}$. Each chlorine atom has seven valence electrons and can take only one, $\ce{Cl + e- -> Cl-}$, so two Cl atoms are needed to take the two electrons, giving $\ce{MgCl2}$. The total positive charge equals the total negative charge in each formula.

questions.solution_md: NaCl; MgCl₂; two electrons need two one-electron acceptors.

marking_scheme.step: NaCl with the transfer of one electron
MgCl₂ with the transfer of two electrons
Reason: each Cl accepts only one electron

questions.stem_md: A student is given the electronegativities (illustrative) Cs 0.7, F 4, C 2.5, Cl 3, Ca 1 and O 3.5. Calculate the difference for each of the bonds Cs–F, C–Cl and Ca–O, and decide which bond is the most ionic and which is the least ionic.

answer.model_answer_md: Differences: Cs–F = 4 − 0.7 = 3.3; C–Cl = 3 − 2.5 = 0.5; Ca–O = 3.5 − 1 = 2.5. The Cs–F bond has the largest difference, so it is the most ionic; the C–Cl bond has the smallest difference (0.5), so it is the least ionic (it is covalent).

questions.solution_md: Cs–F 3.3; C–Cl 0.5; Ca–O 2.5; most ionic Cs–F, least C–Cl.

questions.stem_md:
(a) With the help of electron-dot structures, show how magnesium fluoride is formed from magnesium and fluorine atoms, giving the electronic configuration of each ion formed. [3]

(b) Explain why the formula is MgF₂ and not MgF, and name the noble gas atom to which both ions are isoelectronic. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A magnesium atom (2, 8, 2) has two valence electrons; a fluorine atom (2, 7) has seven. Mg transfers one electron to each of two F atoms: Mg(••) + 2 F(seven dots) → [Mg]²⁺ 2 [F with eight dots]⁻. Mg²⁺ is (2, 8) and each F⁻ is (2, 8), with a full octet.

(b) Magnesium must lose two electrons, but each fluorine atom can accept only one to reach its octet, so two F atoms are needed to take both and the total charge is zero: 2+ and 2 × (1−). Mg²⁺ and F⁻ each have 10 electrons and are isoelectronic with neon.

questions.solution_md: Transfer of 1 electron to each of two F; Mg²⁺ (2, 8) and F⁻ (2, 8); neon.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Electron transfer shown with dot structures
(b) Two F atoms, each accepting one electron

questions.stem_md:
(a) Name three factors that favour the formation of an ionic bond. [3]

(b) The ionisation enthalpy of sodium is 496 kJ mol⁻¹ and the electron gain enthalpy of chlorine is −349 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the enthalpy change for $\ce{Na(g) + Cl(g) -> Na+(g) + Cl-(g)}$ and explain why sodium chloride still forms readily. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) (i) a low ionisation enthalpy of the metal, (ii) a large negative electron gain enthalpy of the non-metal, (iii) a high lattice enthalpy, the energy released when the gaseous ions form the crystal (a large electronegativity difference also favours the transfer).

(b) ΔH = IE + EGE = 496 + (−349) = +147 kJ mol⁻¹. The formation of the ions from the atoms absorbs energy, but when the ions pack into the lattice a large amount of energy (the lattice enthalpy, −788 kJ mol⁻¹) is released, much more than 147 kJ, so the process as a whole is strongly exothermic.

questions.solution_md: Three factors; +147 kJ mol⁻¹ offset by the lattice enthalpy.

questions.stem_md: Sodium forms Na⁺ readily but never Na²⁺ in chemical reactions. The main reason is that:

options.text_md: sodium has only one electron in its whole atom
the second electron of sodium is held less strongly than the first
a Na²⁺ ion would be larger than the Na atom
removing a second electron means breaking into the stable (2, 8) neon-like core, which needs far more energy

questions.solution_md: After the single 3s electron goes, the ion has the stable neon core (2, 8); a second ionisation enthalpy (about 4560 kJ mol⁻¹ against 496) is far too large to be paid by lattice formation — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A sample of iron(II) chloride slowly turns into iron(III) chloride on exposure to chlorine. The extra stability of the Fe³⁺ ion is best explained by its:

options.text_md: completely empty 4s and 3d orbitals
completely filled 3d¹⁰ arrangement
half-filled 3d⁵ arrangement, which is especially stable
noble gas arrangement of eight outer electrons

questions.solution_md: Fe is [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². Fe²⁺ is 3d⁶ and Fe³⁺ is 3d⁵, a half-filled d subshell, which adds to its stability — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Lead(II) compounds are generally more stable than lead(IV) compounds, while carbon prefers the +4 state. The better explanation for lead is:

options.text_md: the two 6s electrons are held tightly and do not take part in bonding (inert pair effect)
lead has only two valence electrons in its outer shell
lead(IV) ions are too small to exist in crystals
lead has no p electrons that could be lost

questions.solution_md: Lead has 6s² 6p². The 6p electrons are lost to give Pb²⁺, but the 6s² pair, poorly shielded and drawn close to the nucleus, resists loss (the inert pair effect) — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Tin (Z = 50) has the outer arrangement 5s² 5p². In the Sn²⁺ ion and in the Sn⁴⁺ ion, the numbers of electrons present are respectively:

options.text_md: 46 and 48
52 and 54
48 and 46
2 and 4

questions.solution_md: Sn²⁺ has 50 − 2 = 48 electrons (the 5p² electrons are lost, 5s² is kept); Sn⁴⁺ has 50 − 4 = 46 (the 5s² pair is lost too) — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Thallium (Group 13, outer arrangement 6s² 6p¹) forms mainly the Tl⁺ ion rather than Tl³⁺. Which statement about the Tl⁺ ion is correct?

options.text_md: It has lost both 6s electrons and kept the 6p electron
It has lost all three outer electrons
It has lost only its 6p electron and keeps the 6s² inert pair
It has gained one electron into the 6p subshell

questions.solution_md: Tl⁺ forms by loss of the single 6p¹ electron; the 6s² pair is held back by the inert pair effect, so Tl⁺ is more stable than Tl³⁺ — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Variable electrovalency of a metal such as iron (Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺) is linked to an "unstable core". This phrase means that, after the outer electrons are removed:

options.text_md: the remaining inner shell, with an incomplete d subshell, is not a stable noble gas core and can lose further electrons
the remaining core is a noble gas arrangement that will not react further
the outer s electrons are held strongly and cannot be removed
the nucleus becomes unstable and decays

questions.solution_md: Fe²⁺ has 3d⁶, not a noble gas core, so one more electron can be lost to give the half-filled Fe³⁺ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A battery-recycling plant handles lead(IV) oxide, which contains the Pb⁴⁺ ion. How many electrons are present in one Pb⁴⁺ ion (atomic number of lead = 82)?
questions.solution_md: A neutral Pb atom has 82 electrons; Pb⁴⁺ has lost four: 82 − 4 = 78.

questions.stem_md: True or false? In its compounds, lead is more stable in the +4 state than in the +2 state.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Because of the inert pair effect the +2 state of lead is more stable; lead(IV) compounds such as PbO₂ are oxidising agents.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Thallium shows the +1 state in most of its compounds.

**Reason (R):** The 6s² electrons of thallium are reluctant to take part in bonding.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both true. The inert 6s² pair stays behind and only the 6p¹ electron is lost, so R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: What is meant by the inert pair effect? Give one metal that shows it and the two oxidation states it commonly has.

answer.model_answer_md: In heavy p-block elements the two ns electrons are held strongly by the nucleus (poorly shielded by the d and f electrons) and do not take part in bonding, so the lower oxidation state, two less than the group valence, becomes more stable. Lead (6s² 6p²) shows +2 and +4, with +2 the more stable; thallium (+1 and +3) and tin (+2 and +4) are other examples.

questions.solution_md: ns² pair not used; Pb +2 and +4.

marking_scheme.step: Example with its two oxidation states

questions.stem_md: Write the electronic configurations of Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ (atomic number of Fe = 26) and say which ion is the more stable towards further change, giving the reason.

answer.model_answer_md: Fe: [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². Fe²⁺: [Ar] 3d⁶. Fe³⁺: [Ar] 3d⁵. Fe³⁺ is the more stable, because its 3d subshell is exactly half-filled (five unpaired electrons), which gives extra stability.

questions.solution_md: Fe²⁺ 3d⁶; Fe³⁺ 3d⁵, half-filled, more stable.

questions.stem_md: Why is a cation always smaller than its parent atom, and an anion always larger? Answer for Mg and Mg²⁺ and for Cl and Cl⁻.

answer.model_answer_md: Mg²⁺ has lost the whole outer shell (n = 3), and its 12 protons now hold only 10 electrons more strongly, so the ion is smaller than the atom. In Cl⁻ one extra electron is added to the same shell, so the electron–electron repulsion rises while the nuclear charge (17+) is unchanged; the electron cloud expands and the ion is larger than the atom.

questions.solution_md: Cation: fewer shells and more pull per electron; anion: more repulsion, same nuclear charge.

questions.stem_md: Tin (outer arrangement 5s² 5p²) forms SnCl₂ and SnCl₄. Give the oxidation state of tin in each, explain how each ion arises and say which state is the more stable for tin, in view of the inert pair effect.

answer.model_answer_md: In SnCl₂ tin is +2 (Sn²⁺) and in SnCl₄ it is +4 (Sn⁴⁺). Sn²⁺ arises when the two 5p electrons are lost, keeping the 5s² pair; Sn⁴⁺ needs the 5s² pair to be lost as well. For tin the 5s² pair is only partly inert, so both states are known (SnCl₂ is a reducing agent, and Sn⁴⁺ compounds are common), but the +2 state becomes steadily more stable going down the group to lead.

questions.solution_md: Sn +2 (5p lost) and +4 (5s also lost); inert pair favours +2 down the group.

marking_scheme.step: Comment on inert pair and stability

questions.stem_md: Explain, with reference to the "unstable core", why iron forms Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ but sodium forms only Na⁺.

answer.model_answer_md: Sodium loses its single 3s electron and the ion is left with the stable noble gas core (2, 8); removing a further electron would break into this core and needs a very large energy, so only Na⁺ forms. Iron loses its two 4s electrons to give Fe²⁺ ([Ar] 3d⁶), but this core is not a noble gas arrangement: it has an incomplete 3d subshell, so a 3d electron can be lost relatively easily to give Fe³⁺ ([Ar] 3d⁵, half-filled and stable). The unstable core therefore leads to variable electrovalency.

questions.solution_md: Na: stable neon core; Fe: incomplete d core, loses a d electron for half-filled d⁵.

marking_scheme.step: Fe²⁺ core is unstable, d electron lost

questions.stem_md: Red lead is Pb₃O₄, a mixed oxide that contains lead in two oxidation states. Using the inert pair effect, state the two oxidation states, say in which ratio they occur in the formula, and name the electrons lost in the higher state.

answer.model_answer_md: The oxidation states are +2 and +4: Pb₃O₄ is 2 PbO · PbO₂, so two Pb²⁺ and one Pb⁴⁺ balance four O²⁻ (2 × 2 + 4 = 8). In Pb²⁺ only the 6p² electrons are lost, the 6s² pair being inert. The Pb⁴⁺ ion has lost the 6s² pair as well as the 6p² electrons.

questions.solution_md: Pb²⁺ : Pb⁴⁺ = 2 : 1; Pb⁴⁺ has also lost the 6s² pair.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is meant by variable electrovalency? Give two examples of elements that show it. [2]

(b) Explain the variable electrovalency of (i) iron and (ii) lead, writing the configurations of the ions concerned. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Variable electrovalency is the ability of an element to form more than one stable cation, that is, to show more than one electrovalency in its compounds. Examples are iron (Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺) and lead (Pb²⁺ and Pb⁴⁺).

(b) (i) Iron is [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². It loses the two 4s electrons to give Fe²⁺ ([Ar] 3d⁶); this core is not a stable noble gas core (unstable core), and a 3d electron is lost to give Fe³⁺ ([Ar] 3d⁵), which is half-filled and stable. (ii) Lead is [Xe] 4f¹⁴ 5d¹⁰ 6s² 6p². Loss of the two 6p electrons gives Pb²⁺ (6s²); the 6s² pair is held tightly (inert pair effect), so Pb²⁺ is stable, but if the pair is lost too, Pb⁴⁺ is formed.

questions.solution_md: Definition with two examples; Fe from the unstable core; Pb from the inert pair.

questions.stem_md: The lattice enthalpy of a crystalline ionic compound such as sodium chloride is the enthalpy change when:

options.text_md: one mole of the solid is formed from its elements in their standard states
one mole of the solid is formed from its gaseous ions, a process that releases energy
one mole of the solid dissolves in a large volume of water
one mole of the solid is formed from its gaseous atoms

questions.solution_md: Lattice enthalpy: $\ce{Na+(g) + Cl-(g) -> NaCl(s)}$, one mole of solid from gaseous ions, with a negative sign for the formation convention — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A materials student compares the lattice enthalpies of NaCl, KCl, MgO and CaO (formation from gaseous ions; values in kJ mol⁻¹: NaCl −788, KCl −717, MgO −3791, CaO −3401). The largest magnitude belongs to MgO because:

options.text_md: both ions carry a single charge and the ions are large
it has the largest ionic radii of the four
both ions carry a double charge and the ions are small, so the attraction is strongest
it contains the smallest number of ions in the lattice

questions.solution_md: MgO (−3791) has Mg²⁺ and O²⁻, ions of high charge and small radius, so the electrostatic attraction (and the energy released on forming the lattice) is the greatest — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The sodium halides NaF, NaCl, NaBr and NaI contain the anions F⁻, Cl⁻, Br⁻ and I⁻ with radii 133, 181, 196, 220 pm. The order of the magnitude of their lattice enthalpies is:

options.text_md: NaI > NaBr > NaCl > NaF
NaCl > NaF > NaI > NaBr
all four are equal, since the cation is the same
NaF > NaCl > NaBr > NaI

questions.solution_md: The same cation, but the anions get larger from F⁻ to I⁻, so the distance between ion centres grows and the attraction falls: NaF > NaCl > NaBr > NaI (−923, −788, −752, −700 kJ mol⁻¹) — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In the Born–Haber cycle for sodium chloride, which of the following steps is exothermic?

options.text_md: $\ce{Na(s) -> Na(g)}$, the sublimation of sodium
$\ce{Cl(g) + e- -> Cl-(g)}$, the electron gain by chlorine
$\ce{Na(g) -> Na+(g) + e-}$, the ionisation of sodium
$\ce{Cl(g) -> Cl+(g) + e-}$, the ionisation of chlorine

questions.solution_md: Sublimation and ionisation absorb energy; the electron gain by chlorine (−349 kJ mol⁻¹) releases it (besides the lattice formation) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A technician tests four white crystalline solids. Which observation is NOT expected for a typical ionic compound?

options.text_md: high melting point and hardness
low melting point and a soft, waxy texture
brittleness when struck with a hammer
good electrical conduction when molten

questions.solution_md: Strong electrostatic forces give ionic solids high melting points, hardness and brittleness, and the melt conducts. A low melting point and waxy softness suggest weak forces, so it is not typical — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A white solid does not conduct electricity when dry, but conducts when melted and when dissolved in water. The solid is most likely:

options.text_md: a metal, whose delocalised electrons are free only in the melt
a covalent network solid, whose atoms become free in water
a non-polar molecular solid, whose molecules ionise in the melt
an ionic compound, whose ions are free to move in the melt and in solution

questions.solution_md: In the solid, ions are fixed in the lattice. In the melt and in solution they move, carrying current — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A crystal of sodium chloride shatters when struck sharply with a hammer. The best explanation is that:

options.text_md: the ions are held by very weak forces and slide apart easily
the crystal contains free electrons that heat up on impact
the ions are attracted more strongly when the layers shift
a shift of one layer brings ions of like charge face to face, and their repulsion splits the crystal

questions.solution_md: Displacing a layer by one ion width puts Na⁺ opposite Na⁺ and Cl⁻ opposite Cl⁻; repulsion splits the crystal along that plane, so ionic solids are brittle — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Most ionic compounds dissolve in water because the polar water molecules surround the ions and the energy released on hydration helps to overcome the lattice enthalpy.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. Hydration of the ions releases energy that compensates for the energy needed to separate them from the lattice; non-polar solvents cannot do this.

questions.stem_md: Ionic solids have high melting points because of the strong ___ forces between the oppositely charged ions in the lattice.
questions.solution_md: Strong electrostatic (coulombic) attraction between the ions must be overcome to melt the solid.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Sodium chloride forms readily from sodium and chlorine even though the formation of gaseous Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions from atoms absorbs energy.

**Reason (R):** The energy released when the gaseous ions pack into the lattice is larger than the energy absorbed in making them.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true: Na(g) + Cl(g) → Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g) needs +147 kJ mol⁻¹, but the lattice enthalpy, −788 kJ mol⁻¹, outweighs it. R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Match each property of sodium chloride with the feature of its structure that accounts for it.

options.text_md: High melting point
Brittleness
Conducts when molten
Does not conduct as a solid

match_right.text_md: like ions meet when layers slide

questions.solution_md: High melting point → s; brittleness → p; conducts when molten → q; no conduction as a solid → r.

questions.stem_md: A thermochemistry student builds the Born–Haber cycle for potassium chloride. The data (kJ mol⁻¹) are: enthalpy of formation of KCl(s) −437, sublimation of K 89, dissociation of Cl₂ 242 (per mole of Cl₂), first ionisation enthalpy of K 419, electron gain enthalpy of Cl −349. Calculate the lattice enthalpy of KCl in kJ mol⁻¹.
questions.solution_md: $\Delta H_\text{f} = \Delta H_\text{sub} + \tfrac12 D(\ce{Cl-Cl}) + \text{IE} + \text{EGE} + U$, so $U = -437 - (89 + 121 + 419 - 349) = -437 - 280 = -717$ kJ mol⁻¹.

marking_scheme.step: Uses ½ of the Cl–Cl dissociation enthalpy: 121

questions.stem_md: A fluoride-toothpaste researcher needs the enthalpy of formation of sodium fluoride. Data (kJ mol⁻¹): sublimation of Na 108, dissociation of F₂ 158 (per mole of F₂), ionisation enthalpy of Na 496, electron gain enthalpy of F −328, lattice enthalpy of NaF −923. Calculate the enthalpy of formation of NaF(s).

marking_scheme.step: Adds all five terms with signs

questions.stem_md: The Born–Haber cycle for sodium bromide has the data (kJ mol⁻¹): enthalpy of formation −361, lattice enthalpy −752, sublimation of Na 108, enthalpy of atomisation of ½Br₂(l) to Br(g) 112, ionisation enthalpy of Na 496. Calculate the electron gain enthalpy of bromine.
questions.solution_md: $\text{EGE} = \Delta H_\text{f} - U - (\Delta H_\text{sub} + \Delta H_\text{atom} + \text{IE}) = -361 - (-752) - (108 + 112 + 496) = 391 - 716 = -325$ kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.stem_md: Define the lattice enthalpy of an ionic solid. On which law is the Born–Haber cycle based?

answer.model_answer_md: The lattice enthalpy is the enthalpy change when one mole of the crystalline solid is formed from its constituent gaseous ions, e.g. $\ce{Na+(g) + Cl-(g) -> NaCl(s)}$, $\Delta H = -788$ kJ mol⁻¹ (it is the energy released). The Born–Haber cycle is based on Hess's law: the enthalpy of formation is the same whether the compound is made directly from its elements or by the stepwise route through atoms, ions and the lattice.

questions.solution_md: Gaseous ions to one mole of solid; Hess’s law.

questions.stem_md: Give two characteristics of ionic compounds and relate each to the structure of the solid.

answer.model_answer_md: Ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points, since a lot of energy is needed to overcome the strong electrostatic attractions between the oppositely charged ions in the lattice. They conduct electricity when molten or dissolved but not as solids, since the ions are free to move only in the melt or solution, and are fixed in the lattice in the solid.

questions.solution_md: High melting point from strong attractions; conduction only when ions are free.

marking_scheme.step: First property with the structural reason
Second property with the structural reason

questions.stem_md: Magnesium oxide melts at about 2850 °C, but sodium chloride melts at about 800 °C. Explain the difference in terms of the charges and sizes of the ions.

answer.model_answer_md: Both have the same type of lattice, but MgO contains Mg²⁺ and O²⁻, ions with double charges, and the ions are smaller (72 and 140 pm) than the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions (102 and 181 pm). The attraction between ions, proportional to the product of the charges and falling with distance, is therefore much stronger in MgO (lattice enthalpy about −3791 kJ mol⁻¹ against −788 kJ mol⁻¹), so far more energy is needed to melt it.

questions.solution_md: Higher charges and smaller ions: much larger lattice enthalpy for MgO.

marking_scheme.step: Stronger attraction, larger lattice enthalpy, higher melting point

questions.stem_md: List the five steps of the Born–Haber cycle for the formation of NaCl(s) from Na(s) and Cl₂(g), writing an equation for each step and naming the enthalpy change.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) Sublimation of sodium: $\ce{Na(s) -> Na(g)}$ (sublimation enthalpy). (2) Dissociation of chlorine: $\ce{1/2 Cl2(g) -> Cl(g)}$ (half the bond dissociation enthalpy). (3) Ionisation of sodium: $\ce{Na(g) -> Na+(g) + e-}$ (ionisation enthalpy). (4) Electron gain by chlorine: $\ce{Cl(g) + e- -> Cl-(g)}$ (electron gain enthalpy). (5) Formation of the lattice: $\ce{Na+(g) + Cl-(g) -> NaCl(s)}$ (lattice enthalpy). By Hess's law the sum of steps 1–5 equals the enthalpy of formation of NaCl(s).

questions.solution_md: Five steps with equations; sum = ΔHf.

marking_scheme.step: Step 5 and the Hess’s law statement

questions.stem_md: In a Born–Haber cycle for magnesium chloride the data (kJ mol⁻¹) are: ΔHf of MgCl₂(s) −641; sublimation of Mg 148; dissociation of Cl₂ 242; first and second ionisation enthalpies of Mg 738 and 1451; electron gain enthalpy of Cl −349. Calculate the lattice enthalpy of MgCl₂.

answer.model_answer_md: Atoms of Cl needed: 2, from 1 mol of Cl₂: dissociation $= 242$. Electron gain: $2 \times (-349) = -698$. Sum of steps $= 148 + 242 + 738 + 1451 + (-698) = 1881$ kJ mol⁻¹. $U = \Delta H_\text{f} - 1881 = -641 - 1881 = -2522$ kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.solution_md: Sum of steps $= 1881$ kJ mol⁻¹; $U = -2522$ kJ mol⁻¹.

marking_scheme.step: Two Cl atoms: 242 for dissociation and 2 × (−349) for electron gain

questions.stem_md: The lattice enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹) of LiF, NaF and KCl are −1037, −923 and −717. Arrange them in order of magnitude and explain the order using the sizes of the ions (Li⁺ 76, Na⁺ 102, K⁺ 138, F⁻ 133, Cl⁻ 181 pm).

answer.model_answer_md: The order of magnitude is LiF (−1037) > NaF (−923) > KCl (−717). All three have ions of single charge, so the difference depends on the distance between the ion centres. The distances are Li⁺ + F⁻ = 209 pm, Na⁺ + F⁻ = 235 pm, K⁺ + Cl⁻ = 319 pm. The shorter the distance, the stronger the attraction and the larger the lattice enthalpy.

questions.solution_md: LiF > NaF > KCl; ion-centre distances 209, 235, 319 pm.

marking_scheme.step: Sum of radii for each compound

questions.stem_md: Sodium chloride is hard and brittle, has a high melting point and conducts electricity only in the molten or dissolved state. Explain each observation.

answer.model_answer_md: High melting point and hardness: the oppositely charged ions are held in a regular lattice by strong electrostatic forces, which need a large amount of energy to overcome. Brittleness: a blow shifts a layer so that ions of like charge come face to face and repel, splitting the crystal. Conduction: in the solid the ions are fixed and cannot carry current; when melted or dissolved the ions are free to move, so the liquid conducts.

questions.solution_md: Strong lattice forces; like-ion repulsion on slipping; free ions in melt or solution.

marking_scheme.step: High melting point and hardness explained

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw, or describe in steps with equations, the Born–Haber cycle for the formation of potassium chloride from solid potassium and chlorine gas. [3]

(b) Use the data (kJ mol⁻¹): ΔHf of KCl(s) −437, sublimation of K 89, ½ × Cl–Cl dissociation 121, ionisation of K 419, electron gain of Cl −349, to calculate the lattice enthalpy of KCl. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\ce{K(s) -> K(g)}$ (sublimation); $\ce{1/2 Cl2(g) -> Cl(g)}$ (dissociation); $\ce{K(g) -> K+(g) + e-}$ (ionisation); $\ce{Cl(g) + e- -> Cl-(g)}$ (electron gain); $\ce{K+(g) + Cl-(g) -> KCl(s)}$ (lattice formation). By Hess's law the sum of these five enthalpy changes equals the enthalpy of formation of KCl(s) from K(s) and ½Cl₂(g).

(b) $-437 = 89 + 121 + 419 + (-349) + U$, so $U = -437 - 280 = -717$ kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.solution_md: Five steps (Hess's law); U = -717 kJ mol⁻¹.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Ionisation and electron gain with equations

questions.stem_md:
(a) State three characteristics of electrovalent (ionic) compounds and relate each to the structure of the crystal. [3]

(b) A student finds that a white solid melts at 770 °C, is hard and brittle, and its aqueous solution conducts, but the dry solid does not. Is it ionic? Say what the data tell about the ions in the solid and in solution. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) (i) High melting and boiling points: strong electrostatic attraction between the ions in the lattice must be overcome. (ii) Brittle and hard: the lattice is rigid; a shift of a layer brings like charges together and the crystal splits. (iii) Conduct electricity only when molten or dissolved: the ions are fixed in the solid and free to move in the melt or in solution. (Also soluble in polar solvents such as water, insoluble in non-polar solvents.)

(b) Yes, the evidence points to an ionic solid. The ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice (no conduction, high melting point and brittleness), but when dissolved in water they are surrounded by water molecules and move freely, so the solution conducts.

questions.solution_md: Three properties with structural reasons; the data indicate an ionic solid.

questions.stem_md:
(a) The data (kJ mol⁻¹) for sodium chloride are: sublimation of Na 108, ½ × Cl–Cl dissociation 121, ionisation of Na 496, electron gain of Cl −349, lattice enthalpy −788. Calculate the standard enthalpy of formation of NaCl(s). [3]

(b) Which of the steps in (a) is the largest in magnitude, and why must it be so large for the compound to be stable? [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) ΔHf = 108 + 121 + 496 + (−349) + (−788) = 376 + (−788) = −412 kJ mol⁻¹.

(b) The lattice enthalpy (−788 kJ mol⁻¹) is the largest in magnitude. The steps that make the ions from the atoms absorb 376 kJ mol⁻¹, so the energy released when the ions form the lattice must exceed this for the compound to be more stable than the elements.

questions.solution_md: ΔHf = −412 kJ mol⁻¹; the lattice enthalpy is largest and pays for the endothermic steps.
